la:verb:desero.html:
dē-sĕro, no
perf., sĭtum, 3, v. a., to sow, plant: desitis seminibus,.

la:verb:desidero.gloss: to want, desire, wish for, long for
senses: to want, desire, wish for, long for
to be lost, to be missing
la:verb:desidero.html:
dē-sīdĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
etym. dub.; cf. considero
,
to long for, greatly wish for, to desire something not possessed (freq. and class.—for syn. cf.: opto, requiro, expeto, appeto, affecto, cupio, concupisco, aveo, gestio, capto, volo).
In gen., with acc.: Dies noctesque me ames, me desideres,: quam tu filium tuom, tam pater me meus desiderat,: natura quid velit, anquirat, desideret,: nec sitio honores, nec desidero gloriam,: dum illa desideramus, ab aliis avertimur,: quid desideremus aut deprecemur,: nec nunc vires desidero adolescentis non plus quam adolescens tauri aut elephanti desiderabam,; : desiderantem quod satis est,: Sextilem totum mendax desideror, et saep.—
With acc. and inf.: me gratiam aps te inire verbis nil desidero,: mihi dari haud desidero,: quo ullam rem ad se importari desiderent,.— With inf. alone: mori,.—
With ab or in: ab Chrysippo nihil magnum desideravi,; ; : ab milite modestiam et continentiam,: in quo (Catone) summam eloquentiam,; ; ; ; —
Absol.: misere amans desiderat,; ; —
Of inanimate subjects: desiderarunt te oculi mei,: nullam virtus aliam mercedem laborum desiderat praeter, etc.,: ut desiderat laus probationem, sic, etc., et saep.: desiderant rigari arbores,.
With predominant idea of lacking, wanting, to miss any thing: ex me audies, quid in oratione tua desiderem,: si non est, nolis esse neque desideres,: quid a peritioribus rei militaris desiderari videbatur, et saep.—Esp. with quominus: praeter quercum Dodonaeam nihil desideramus, quo minus Epirum ipsum possidere videamur,. —
Meton.(effectus pro causa), to lose something; and more freq. pass., to be missing, to be lost: in eo proelio non amplius CC milites desideravit,; cf. : ut nulla navis desideraretur,; et saep.: neque quicquam ex fano praeter unum signum desideratum est,; : ex peditibus triginta,.—
With the notion of inquiring, searching; to investigate, examine, discuss (rare): sequitur ut morbo laborantibus remedia desiderentur,: examina,.—Impers.: antequam desideraretur,before the question should be raised,.—Hence,
dēsīdĕrans, antis, P. a., in Sup. desiderantissimus, in the later writers for desideratissimus, as a term of endearment, heart's desire, best beloved: vale, domine dulcissime, desiderantissime,; M. Aur. ; L. Aur. Verus,; .— Adv.: dēsīdĕranter, acc. to no. I., with desire, eagerly (late Lat.): appetere,.—Comp.: quanto desiderantius desideras,.—
dēsīdĕrātus, a, um, P. a., wished for, longed for, welcome (very rare): et veniet desideratus cunctis gentibus,: blandissima et desideratissimi promissa. : fratres desideratissimi,; and in inscrr. applied to a beloved person: FILIO DESIDERATISSIMO,;

la:verb:desido.html:
dē-sīdo, sēdi (de-sīdi, Cic. l. l. infra, Lampr ), 3, v. n., v. consido. —Of inanimate things, esp. of places,
to sink, fall, or settle down.
Prop.: tantos terrae motus factos esse, ut multa oppida corruerint, multis locis labes factae sint terraeque desiderint,; ; ; and poet. of the apparent sinking of mountains to one flying aloft: Gargara desidunt surgenti,: ovum inane natat, plenum desidit,; : ex urina quod desidit album est,sediment,: tumor ex toto desidit,. —*
Trop., to deteriorate, degenerate: desidentes mores, Liv. prooem. 9.

senses: to fall short of, fail to obtain, miss
to abandon, to desert, to neglect
to be away, to be absent, to be missing
la:verb:desum.html:
dē-sum, fŭi, esse (ee in deest, deesse, deerit, etc., in the poets
per synaeresin as one syll., ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; praes. subj., desiet, ; perf., defuerunt, trisyl., ; fut. inf., commonly defuturum esse, as , etc.; also defore,; ; ; imperf. subj., deforent, ), v. n., to be away, be absent; to fail, be wanting (for syn. cf.: absum, deficio, descisco, negligo; freq. in all periods).
In gen.
Absol.: non ratio, verum argentum deerat,: frigore enim desunt ignes ventique calore Deficiunt,: cf. ; : omnia deerant, quae, etc.,: semper paullum ad summam felicitatem defuisse,: ibi numquam causas seditionum et certaminis defore,: quod non desit habentem, etc., et saep.: non desunt qui, for sunt qui,; ; .—
With dat. (so most freq.): metuo mihi in monendo ne defuerit oratio, and 4: cui nihil desit, quod, etc.,; cf. : sive deest naturae quippiam, sive abundat atque affluit,: quantum alteri sententiae deesset animi, tantum alteri superesse,; so, opp. superesse,; cf. opp. superare,: neu desint epulis rosae,; et saep.: hoc unum ad pristinam fortunam Caesari defuit,; cf. ; . —
With in: ut neque in Antonio deesset hic ornatus orationis, neque in Crasso redundaret,; : in C. Laenio commendando,—
With inf. (poet. and in postAug. prose): et mihi non desunt turpes pendere corollae,; ; —(ε) With quominus: duas sibi res, quominus in vulgus et in foro diceret, defuisse, (ap. ); .—(ζ) With quin: nihil contumeliarum defuit, quin subiret,.—(η) With ut: non defuit, ut, etc.,.—
Pregn., to fail, be wanting in one's duty, as in rendering assistance, etc.; not to assist or serve, to desert one, to neglect a person or thing.
With dat.: tantum enitor, ut neque amicis neque etiam alienioribus opera, consilio, labore desim,; cf. : ne tibi desis,that you be not wanting to yourself, neglect not your own advantage,; ; cf. ; ; : senatu reique publicae,: communi saluti nulla in re,: Timotheo de fama dimicanti,: huic rei,: negotio,: decori vestro,: officio et dignitati meae,; : tempori,; cf.: occasioni temporis, et saep.—
Without dat.: non deest reipublicae consilium ... nos, nos, dico aperte, consules desumus,; : qui non deerat in causis,: nec deerat Ptolemaeus,—
To fall short of, miss, fail to obtain: ne quis desit gratiae Dei,.

la:noun:desperatio.html:
dēspērātĭo, ōnis, f.
despero
,
hopelessness, despair: desperatio est aegritudo sine ulla rerum exspectatione meliorum,.
Prop. (good prose and very freq.).
With gen.: omnium rerum amissio et desperatio recuperandi,: omnium rerum, (opp. bona spes); ; et saep.: victoriae,: magna pacis,: omnium salutis,; et saep.—
Absol.: magna desperatione affectus,: ad summam desperationem pervenire,: ad desperationem adducti,; cf.: ad desperationem redactus,: in desperatione esse,: ad desperationem formidine properare, et saep.: a desperatione iram accendit,; cf. —In plur.: desperationes eorum, qui, etc.,.—
Meton., desperate boldness, foolhardiness: desperatio truculentae feminae, Ap. M. 10, p. 251: periculosa,; id. Sirach, 27, 24.

la:verb:destituo.gloss: to fix or set in position; to place
senses: to fix or set in position; to place
to leave alone, forsake, abandon or desert
la:verb:destituo.html:
dē-stĭtŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a.
statuo
.
To set down; to set, place anywhere (ante-class. and freq. in Liv.; elsewh. rare): destituit omnes servos ad mensam ante se, Caecil. ap. : navem in alto ancoris, Naev. ib.: palum in foro, C. Gracchus ap. : aliquem in convivio (sc. ludendi causa),: armatos in medio,: aliquem ante tribunal,; cf. : cohortes extra vallum,: duo signa hic, et saep.—Far more freq. and class.,
(Lit., to put away from one's self; hence) To leave alone, to forsake, abandon, desert (derelinquo, desero, q. v.): T. Roscius novem homines honestissimos induxit, decepit, destituit, adversariis tradidit,: destitutus ab aliquo,; ; cf. : funditores inermes,: aliquem in septemviratu,; cf.: defensores in ipso discrimine periculi, et saep.: inceptam fugam,to desist from,: morando spem,: spem vindemiae,: consilium,: honorem,: conata ejus,: partem verborum, to pronounce indistinctly (with devorare), Spald. et saep.—Poet., with acc. and abl.: ex quo destituit deos Mercede pactā Laomedon, i. e. defrauded of their stipulated reward, * .—
Of inanimate and abstract subjects: neque reperias, quos aut pronior fortuna comitata sit, aut, veluti fatigata, maturius destituerit, quam, etc.,: cum primas spes fortuna destituit,; cf. : ventus aliquem,: aliquem vadum,: aliquem poplites,; cf.: aliquem memoria, mens,: alveum fluitantem aqua,; cf.: freta destituent nudos in litore pisces, * .—
Part. perf. destitutus, constr. usu. ab aliquo, aliquā re, rarely ab aliquā re, freq. with ab, abandoned, forsaken by; robbed of, destitute of: in divite ac paupere: propinquis, amicis, clientibus abundante, et his omnibus destituto,: alicujus consiliis, promissis, praeceptis destitutus,: scientiā juris,: lenociniis, et saep.; but with spe, a is more freq.: destituti ab unica spe auxilii,: a spe,; ; (with spe, ): a re familiari,.—
Absol.: si is destituat, nihil satis tutum habebis,: simul, si destituat spes, alia praesidia molitur,; so, spes,; : pietasque fidesque,: ego,.

la:verb:desino.gloss: to leave off, give over, give up
senses: to leave off, give over, give up
to stop, end, close, make an end
la:verb:desino.html:
dē-sĭno, sĭi (rarely īvi, , v. Neue, Form. II. 404; also,
sync. perf.: desit,: desisse,; ; ; : desissem, Catull. 36, 5 al.: DESI, dissyl.,), sĭtum, 3, v. a. and n.—Prop., to put or set down; hence, to leave off, give over, cease, desist (opp. coepi, the construction of which it for the most part follows; cf. for syn.: cesso, cunctor, tergiversor, defugio, haesito, moror, tardor; desisto, omitto, intermitto, praetermitto, praetereo, etc.).
Act.
With inf. act.: illud jam mirari desino,: te uti teste,: commemorare eos,: amare,: lacessere,: maledicere,: de compositione loqui, * et saep.—Less freq.,
with inf. pass.: ubi ipsi Desierunt vorti,: moveri,: fieri,: cerni,: quaeri ab eo,: inquiri,—
With acc. (mostly poet.): artem,; ; : seditionem,: versus,; cf. plura,; 9, 66: Titania bella,: lugubres voces, Ap. Mag. 5, p.170 al.—
Pass. (usually in the tempp. perff.): veteres orationes a plerisque legi sunt desitae,; cf. ; and: Persei numquam desitum celebrari nomen,: censores creari desitos,: sermone abhinc multis annis jam desito,: nectier postea desitum,; cf. : coeptum per eos qui volebant, desitum est per hunc, qui decessit, id. Cornel. Fragm. ap. P.— In the pres.: tunc bene desinitur,.—
Neutr., to cease, stop, end, close (not freq. till after the Aug. period).
In gen.:' omne bellum sumi facile, ceterum aegerrume desinere, : ferrea primum desinet gens,: desierant imbres,: desinat ira,: cetera, fragilia et caduca occidunt desinuntque,perish, et saep.: cauda desinit in piscem,; cf. ; ; ; : : (gemma) ad vini colorem accedens, prius quam eum degustet, in viola desinit fulgor,: Pyrenaeus desinens,i. e. their extreme end,.—
With abl. and in: in quo desinimus,; or abl. alone: desine quaeso communibus locis,.—With gen., poet. (like the Gr. παύειν and λήγειν): querelarum,: irae,.—Absol.: Mi. Ah! pergisne? De. Jam jam desino, : ut incipiendi (sc. sermonem) ratio fuerit, ita sit desinendi modus,; so opp. incipere,; : quo ex genere coeperis translationes, hoc desinas,: cantasse eum publice Oedipodem exsulem atque in hoc desisse versu: Θανεῖν μʼ ἀνῷγε, etc., : a praeceptis incipio, desino in exemplis,.—In colloq. lang. desine sometimes like the Gr. παῦε (cf. Lidd. and Scott, under παύω, no. II.), leave off! give over! stop! be still! etc.: Ba. Heu, heu, heu! Ps. Desine, ; so ; —
Esp., in rhetor., of the close of a period, to end, close: illa, quae similiter desinunt, etc.,; cf. ; et saep.; cf. cado, no. II.

senses: to cease, desist from (usually coupled with ablative)
la:verb:desisto.html:
dē-sisto, stĭti, stĭtum, 3 (
perf. destitĕrunt, ), v. a. and n. (for syn. v. desino init.).
Act., to set down: in scopulo puellam, Ap. M. 4, p. 157 ().—
Neutr.
To stand off from a thing, to stand apart: quid tu tristis es? quid illa autem abs te irata destitit?.—
Hence, of an action, to leave off, cease, give over, desist from (freq. and class.).—Constr. with de, ab, or simple abl., the dat., the inf., quin, and absol. (in class. prose most freq. with the simple abl., or with the inf.): verbo de sententia destitisti,: de illa mente,: de petitione,: de diutina contentione,: a defensione,; : ab oppugnatione,: ab operibus suis,: hoc conatu,: conatu,: oppugnatione,; : consilio,: negotio,: itinere,: fuga, (with fugere, , v.the foll.): sententia,; : causa,: impio bello,: incepto,; ; .—With dat., poet.: pugnae,: labori,.—With inf.: regem flagitare,: de isdem scribere,: locupletare cives,: causas agere,: mortem timere,: pecuniam polliceri,: Inachia furere,: persequi aliquem, et saep.—With quin: neque, eam quin inveniam, desistam,; Vatin. ap. .—Absol.: desiste; recte ego rem meam sapio,; ; ; et saep.: ter in primo destitit ore sonus,stuck in my throat,; cf. : desistente auctumno,i. e. coming to a close,.
la:verb:desisto.inflection: stĭti, stĭtum, 3, v. a. and n.

la:noun:desiderium.gloss: longing, desire, wish (especially for something once possessed)
senses: longing, desire, wish (especially for something once possessed)
la:noun:desiderium.html:
dēsīdĕrĭum, ii, n.
desidero
,
a longing, ardent desire or wish, properly for something once possessed; grief, regret for the absence or loss of any thing (for syn. cf.: optio, optatio, cupido, cupiditas, studium, appetitio, voluntas—freq. and class.).
Prop.
With gen. object.: te desiderium Athenarum cepisset,; cf.: me desiderium tenet urbis,; ; and, locorum,: rerum earum,; cf. ; : esse in desiderio alicujus,: desiderium conjunctissimi viri ferre,: Scipionis desiderio moveri,: tam cari capitis,: defuncti, et saep.: desiderio id fieri tuo (for tui),; cf.: voluntas, in qua inest aliqua vis desiderii ad sanandum volnus injuriae,.—
Absol.: pectora dura tenet desiderium, Enn. ap. : alicui esse magno desiderio,: explere exspectationem diuturni desiderii,: quo (desiderio) conficior,: ex desiderio laborare,: facere aliquid cum desiderio,: demus hoc desiderio jam pene publico, et saep. In plur.: desideria alicujus commovere, Cic. Rab. perd. 9, 24; et saep.
Trop., of a person, as the object of longing: nunc desiderium, curaque non levis,: desiderio meo nitenti, Catull. 2, 5; and as a term of endearment: mea lux, meum desiderium ... valete, mea desideria, valete,; Catull. 2, 5.—
Transf.
Want, need, necessity,

in general (rare; not ante-Aug.): cibi potionisque desiderium naturale, et saep.: pro desiderio corporum,: desideria scabendi,—

In the time of the empire, a request, petition on the part of inferiors: desideria militum ad Caesarem ferenda,; ; ; ; ; .—
Desires, pleasures (late Lat.): servientibus desideriis et voluptatibus,: carnis,.

la:verb:describo.gloss: to copy off or transcribe something from the original, write down, write out
senses: to copy off or transcribe something from the original, write down, write out
to describe in painting or writing, draw, draw out, sketch off
to mark off, establish, define, divide or distribute into parts
la:verb:describo.html:
dē-scrībo, psi, ptum (in MSS. and edd. often confounded with discribo, q. v.), 3, v. a.
To copy off, transcribe any thing from an original (freq. in Cic.; elsewh. rare): scripsit Balbus ad me, se a te (i. e. e tuo exemplo) quintum de Finibus librum descripsisse,; cf. : epistolam,; , 2; 12, 7, 22: legem,; ; so, to write down, write out: carmina in foliis,; in carved letters: in viridi cortice carmina,.— Class. and far more freq.,
To sketch off, to describe in painting, writing, etc.: delineare, definire.
Lit.: non potuit pictor rectius describere ejus formam,; so, geometricas formas in harena,: formas in pulvere,; cf. ; ; : sphaeram,; cf. caelum,: caeli meatus radio,; cf. : vitam votivā tabellā, et saep.—
Trop.
To represent, delineate, describe: malos mores,; cf.: hominum sermones moresque,: definienda res erit verbis et breviter describenda,fin: qualem (mulierem) ego paulo ante descripsi,; ; : me latronem ac sicarium,: si quis erat dignus describi, quod malus ac fur, etc.,: malo carmine,; : vulnera Parthi,: lucum, aram Dianae, flumen Rhenum, pluvium arcum, et saep.: praecepta,: facta versibus,. —Rarely
with acc. and inf.: nec qui descripsit corrumpi semina matrum,; .—Part. subst.: dēscrip-ta, ōrum, n.: recitari factorum dictorumque ejus descripta per dies jussit,the diary,.—
To mark off, define, divide, distribute into parts. (But whenever the notion of distribution or division is implied, the form discribo seems to have been used by class. writers; and is now restored where de-scr. is found in earlier edd., e.g. ; ; et saep.) Cf.: libertinos in quatuor urbanas tribus,: annum in duodecim menses,; . —Without in.: commode omnes descripti, aetates, classes, equitatus,; and: classes centuriasque et hunc ordinem ex censu descripsit,: terram, et saep.—
Aliquid (alicui), to ascribe, apportion, appoint, assign to any one (cf. remark, no. 2 supra); cf.: vecturas frumenti finitimis civitatibus, * ; : officia,to define,; : vices (poetae),: munera pugnae, et saep.—Hence, dēscrip-tus, a, um, P. a., qs. marked out, i. e. precisely ordered, properly arranged (ap. Cic.): materies orationis omnibus locis descripta, instructa ornataque,; cf.: ordo verborum,: natura nihil est aptius, nihil descriptius,.—Neutr. plur. as subst.: dēscrip-ta, orum, things recorded, writings, .—Sup. does not occur.—* Adv.: dē-scriptē, distinctly, precisely: descripte et electe digerere, opp. confuse et permixte dispergere,.

la:noun:designator.html:
dēsignātor or dissignātor (the latter form freq. in inscrr., and preferred by Brambach; so Keller, ad ; Corp. Inscr. Lat. pp. 597, 768), ōris, m.
id.
,
one who regulates or arranges; a regulator.—As a t. t.,
An officer whose duty it was to assign seats in the theatre, .—
A master of ceremonies at funerals; an undertaker, ; ; ; ; cf. Don. .—
An umpire at public spectacles, i. q. Gr. βραβευτής, ; .

la:verb:despero.html:
dē-spēro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
, to be hopeless; to have no hope of, to despair of, to give up (freq. and class.).—Constr. most freq. with de, the acc., or acc. and inf.; less freq. with the dat. or absol.
With de (in Cic. rarely): de sua virtute aut de ipsius diligentia,: de pugna,: de officio imperatoris,,: de expugnatione,: de salute,: de republica,, D, § 6: de summa rerum,: de se, Planc. ap. ; ; ; ; .—
With acc. (in Caes. only in the part. perf.): honores,: honorem,: rempublicam,: pacem,: voluntariam deditionem,: membra invicti Glyconis,; ; .—In the pass.: sive restituimur, sive desperamur,; : hujus salus desperanda est,; cf.: nil desperandum Teucro duce,: desperatis nostris rebus,; cf. : desperata salute, et saep.: desperato improviso tumultu, et saep.— Middle: desperatis hominibus, who gave themselves up, i. e. were desperately resolved, desperate, .—
With acc. and inf.: ego non despero fore aliquem aliquando, qui, etc.,; ; ; ; et saep.—
With dat.: saluti,: oppido,: rebus tuis,: suis fortunis,: sibi,; : saluti suae,.—(ε) Absol.: sive habes aliquam spem de republica sive desperas,; ; ; prooem. § 2; et saep.: spem habere a tribuno plebis, a senatu desperasse,.—Hence, *
dēspēranter, adv., hopelessly, despairingly: loqui secum,.—
dēspērātus, a, um, P. a., given up, despaired of, irremediable, desperate (most freq. in Cic.): exercitum collectum ex senibus desperatis,: remedium aegrotae ac prope desperatae reipublicae,; cf.: reipublicae morbi,: collegium,: desperatas pecunias exigere, et saep.: desperatos vocant, quia corpori suo minime parcunt (of the Christians),. —Prov.: desperatis Hippocrates vetat adhibere medicinam,.— Comp.: haec nunc multo desperatiora,.—Sup.: perfugium,: spes, Balb. ap. , B, § 2.—* Adv., dēspērātē, desperately: non desperate sollicitus,.
la:verb:despero.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

la:verb:destino.gloss: to bind, fasten, secure, fix, make fast
senses: to bind, fasten, secure, fix, make fast
to establish, determine, resolve, consider, predict, destine
la:verb:destino.html:
dē-stĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
obs. stanare; a particip. stem from root STA, v. sto; and cf.: dono, digno, etc., Corss. 2, 416
,
to make fast, make firm, bind (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense—for syn. cf.: decerno, scisco, statuo, jubeo, constituo, sancio, definio).
Lit.: antemnas ad malos,: rates ancoris,: falces (laqueis),: arcas,; dub., v. destina.—
Trop., to establish, determine, resolve, consider; to design, intend, devote, destine; to appoint, choose, elect (syn.: definire, describere, designare, etc.).
In gen. (in Livy freq. connected with animis, v.the foll.).
With double acc.: aliquem consulem,; cf. : Papirium parem destinant animis Magno Alexandro ducem, si, etc.,; cf.: animis auctorem caedis,: aliquem regem, et saep.—
With inf. or a clause: infectis iis, quae agere destinaverat,; cf. ; : potiorem populi Romani quam regis Persei amicitiam habere,; ; ; ; —
With dat.: sibi aliquid,i. e. to intend purchasing,; : operi destinati possent,: aliquem foro,: me arae,: diem necis alicui,: domos publicis usibus,: quod signum cuique loco, : Anticyram omnem illis,: cados tibi, et saep.—
With ad: tempore locoque ad certamen destinatis,: aliquem ad mortem,: consilia ad bellum,: materiam ad scribendum,: ad omne obsequium destinati,.—(ε) With in: saxo aurove in aliud destinato,: legati in provinciam destinati,: noctem proximam in fugam,.—
In partic.
In the lang. of archers, slingers, etc., to fix upon as a mark, to aim at ( = designare scopum): locum oris,; so .—Transf.: sagittas,to shoot at the mark,.—
In the lang. of trade: sibi aliquid, to fix upon for one's self, to intend to buy: minis triginta sibi puellam destinat,; ; ; Lucil. ap. ; — Hence, dēstĭnātus, a, um, destined, fixed (syn.: fixus, certus).
Adj.: certis quibusdam destinatisque sententiis quasi addicti,: ad horam mortis destinatam,: si hoc bene fixum omnibus destinatumque in animo est,: persona (coupled with certus),; cf. .—Destinatum est alicui, with inf. = certum est, it is one's decision, will; he has determined, ; ; —
Subst.
dēstĭnāta, ae, f., = sponsa, a betrothed female, bride, ; cf. .—
dēs-tĭnātum, i, n.
A mark or aim, ; —
An intended, determined object, design, intention: neque tuis neque Liviae destinatis adversabor,; cf.: destinata retinens,; so : antequam destinata componam,the intended narration,: ad destinatum persequor,the goal of life,: destinata dare, the intentions, dispositions of a will, ; so, ex destinato,adv., designedly, intentionally,; ; ; and in a like sense merely destinato,.—dēstĭ-nātē, adv. la:verb:despondeo.html:
dē-spondĕo, spondi, sponsum, 2 (
perf. despopondisse, ; plqpf. despoponderas, ; with despondi,: despondisse, et saep.), v. a., to promise to give, to promise, pledge.
Lit.
In gen. (rarely): librum alicui,: Syriam homini,: domum, hortos, Baias sibi,: imperium Orientis Romanis,: consulatum,: Tarpeias arces sibi (sc. diripiendas, with promittere), .— Far more freq. and class.,
In partic. t. t., to promise in marriage, to betroth, engage: qui spoponderat filiam, despondisse dicebatur, quod de sponte ejus, id est de voluntate exierat, Müll.: filiam alicui,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : vos uni viro, et saep.—Absol.: placuit despondi (sc. eam),; cf.: sororem suam in tam fortem familiam,; and: filiam suam in divitias maxumas,. —Rarely with sibi: Orestillae filiam sibi, to espouse, Cael. ap. .—Pass. impers.: intus despondebitur,.—
Transf., facete: bibliothecam tuam cave cuiquam despondeas, quamvis acrem amatorem inveneris,.—
Trop.
To promise, give up, devote to: spes reipublicae despondetur anno consulatus tui,: perjuria meritis poenis,.—
With predom. idea of removing, putting away from one's self, to give up, yield, resign. So esp. freq. in Plaut.: animum, to lose courage, to despair, despond: ne lamentetur neve animum despondeat,; ; ; ; ; in the same sense, animos,; ; ; and simply, despondere,: sapientiam,to despair of acquiring wisdom,; cf.: nempe quas spopondi? senses: to free oneself, withdraw, leave, defect, desert, revolt from

la:verb:descisco.html:
dē-scisco, īvi or ĭi, ītum, 3, v. n., orig. a publicist's t. t.
to free one's self from a connection with any one, to withdraw, leave, revolt from, = sciscendo deficere; and with an indication of the terminus, to desert to, go over to any one (class. prose).
Prop.: multae longinquiores civitates ab Afranio desciscunt,; so, ab aliquo,; ; ; ; ; et saep.: ad aliquem (opp. a nobis deficere),; cf.: Praeneste ab Latinis ad Romanos descivit,; and simply: ad aliquem,; ; cf. pass. impers.: quibus invitis descitum ad Samnites erat,; and .—Absol.: cum Fidenae aperte descissent,; ; ; ; ; ; : —
Transf. beyond the political sphere, to depart, deviate, withdraw from a person or thing; to fall off from, be unfaithful to: a nobis desciscere quaeres?: a se ipse,: si Cicero a Demosthene paulum in hac parte descivit,: cur Zeno ab hac antiqua institutione desciverit,; so, a pristina causa, Orell. N. cr.: a veritate,: a natura,: a disciplina,: a virtute,: a consuetudine parentum, et saep.: a vita,to separate, sever one's self, (opp. manere in vita).—Pass. impers.: praecipiti cursu a virtute descitum, ad vitia transcursum,.—Stating the terminus, to fall off to, decline to; to degenerate into: ab excitata fortuna ad inclinatam et prope jacentem,; cf.: ad saevitiam, ad cupiditatem,: in regem (i. e. to degenerate, be transformed), : in monstrum,.—
Of subjects not personal: quis ignorat et eloquentiam et ceteras artes descivisse ab ista vetere gloria,: (vitis) gracili arvo non desciscit,does not degenerate,: semina,.

la:verb:designo.html:
dē-signo or dissigno (the latter form preferred by Brambach in sense II. B. 2. infra; so Keller, ad ; cf. Roby, L. G. 2, p. 384), āvi, ātum, 1,
v. a., to mark out, trace out (freq. in the Aug. per.); to describe, designate, define (for syn. cf.: nomino, appello; voco, dico; facio, coöpto, evoco, prodo, declaro, renuntio, seligo).
Lit.: Aeneas urbem designat aratro,; cf.: moenia fossā,: moenia sulco,; and: oppidum sulco,.— With dat.: finis templo Jovis,; cf.: locum circo,:—vulnere frontem, to mark, ; cf.: nubila ingenti gyro,.—*
Transf., to delineate, design, depict, represent, sc. by embroidering, weaving, etc.: Europen,.—Far more freq.,
Trop.
In gen., to point out, mark, denote by speech; to designate, describe, represent: haec ab hominibus callidis animadversa ac notata, verbis designata,; cf.: affectus velut primis lineis designare,; and: aliquem aliqua oratione,: notat et designat oculis ad caedem unumquemque nostrum,; cf.: aliquem digito,; : decumam ex praeda,: aliquem nota ignaviae,: turpitudinem aliquam,: quem (mundum) alio loco ipse designarit deum,: multa, quae nimiam luxuriam et victoriae fiduciam designarent,.—
In partic.
In a bad sense, to contrive, devise, perpetrate (syn.: exsequi, patrare, perpetrare—very rare): quae designata sint et facta nequitia,; cf.: Illa, quae antehac facta sunt, Omitto; modo quid designavit! Donat.—In a good sense: quid non ebrietas designat,effect, do, accomplish, Orell.—
With access. idea of arrangement, to dispose, regulate, arrange, appoint, ordain, nominate, elect, choose: constituere et designare aliquid,: Anaxagoras primus omnium rerum descriptionem et modum mentis infinitae vi ac ratione designari et confici voluit,to be designed and executed,; cf. .—Esp., to appoint to a public office: aliquem praetorem,: Mamertinum Consulem,: ut ii decemviratum habeant, quos plebs designaverit: oblitus est, nullos ab plebe designari,: Catilina in proximum annum consulatum petebat, sperans si designatus foret, etc.,.—Hence,
Polit. t. t.: dēsig-nātus, elect; applied to a person elected to an office, but who has not yet entered upon it: consul,; , and the superscriptions of letters in -8: tribunus plebis,; ; : quaestor, et saep.—Also, said of the office itself: Pompeio consulatus designatus est,.—
Transf., expected; of a child not yet born: designatus civis,.

la:verb:despicio.html:
dē-spĭcĭo, exi, ectum, 3 (
inf. perf. despexe, ), v. n. and a.
To look down upon any thing (for syn. cf.: contemno, sperno, aspernor).
Lit. (mestly poet.).
Neutr.: ad te per impluvium tuum, ; : de vertice montis in valles,: a summo caelo in aequora,: medios in agros,: in vias,—Absol.: vultus suspicientis et despicientis,.—Pass. impers.: colles, qua despici poterat,; ; .—
Act.: si quis Pacuviano invehens curru multas et varias gentis et urbis despicere et oculis conlustrare possit,: Juppiter aethere summo Despiciens mare velivolum terrasque jacentis, etc., (v. Conington ad loc.); cf. ; : e tumulis subjectam urbem,: culmine cuncta,: cavā montis convalle, (Forb. ad loc.): quos (populos) despicit Arctos,.—(Acc. to Lachm. ad Lucr. vol. 2, p. 236, despicio with acc. always has the trop. force, to despise; and in all these passages should be read dispicere; and so Rib. in Verg., Munro ad ; cf. dispicio.)—
Trop. as v. act., to look down upon, to despise, disdain (class. and very freq. —syn.: contemnere, spernere): ut omnes despiciat, ut hominem prae se neminem putet,; cf. ; : divitias (with contemnere honores),: suos,; ipsos,: legionem propter paucitatem,; cf. copias,; : paucitatem militum,; : ullum laborem aut munus,to disdain, decline, shun, et saep.: dum despicis omnes,; et saep.—In part. perf.: homines despecti et contempti,; cf.: huic despecto saluti fuit, (corresp. with contemptus and contemnentibus).—Partic. with the gen.: despiciens sui,extr.; and poet.: despectus taedae,.—*
To look away, not to regard, not to attend: simul atque ille despexerit,.— Hence, P. a., dēspectus, a, um, contemptible, despicable: natura ejus,: Euphrates, ingens modo, inde tenuis rivus, despectus emoritur, Mela, 3, 8, 5.—Comp.: improbos despectiores facere, Boëth. Cons. Phil. 3, pros. 4, p. 47 Obbar.

la:verb:descendo.gloss: to climb down, to go or come down, to descend

la:verb:descendo.html:
dē-scendo, di, sum, 3 (
perf. redupl.: descendidit, Valer. Antias ap. ; and, descendiderant, Laber. ib.; perf.: desciderunt, Inscr. Frat. Arv. 13 Henzen.), v. n., to come down; and of inanimate subjects, to fall, sink down, to descend, opp. to ascendo (class. and freq.).
Lit.
In gen.: ex equo,to alight,; Auct. B. Hisp. 15, 2; for which, equo,: sicut monte descenderat,: e curru,: e tribunali,: de rostris,: de templo,: de caelo,; for which, caelo,: e caelo,: caelo ab alto,; cf.: vertice montis ab alto,; and: ab Histro (Da cus),: ab Alpibus,; : monte,: aggeribus Alpinis atque arce Monoeci,: antro Castalio,: per clivum, et saep.—Indicating the terminus ad quem: in mare de caelo,: Juppiter in terras,: in pon tum,; ; cf.: caelo in hibernas undas,: caelo ad suos honores templaque, etc.,: in aestum,: in inferiorem ambulationem,: in campos,; cf. : in Piraeum, et saep.: ad naviculas,: ad genitorem imas Erebi descendit ad umbras,: sinus vestis infra genua, et saep. Poet. also with dat.: nocti, i. e. ad inferos,; cf. Erebo,.—With sup.: per quod oraculo utentes sciscitatum deos descendunt,.—Absol.: turbo descendit,; cf. : asta ut descendam (sc. ex equo),dismount, alight,; : descendens (sc. e lecto),: descendo (sc. de arce),: umbrae descendentes (sc. ad inferos),.—Poet.: trepidi quoties nos descendentis arenae vidimus in partes, i. e. that seemed to sink as the wild beasts rose from the vaults, .—
In partic.
To go down, to go, to come, sc. from the dwelling-houses (which in Rome were mostly situated on eminences) to the forum, the comitia, etc.: in forum descendens, Crass. ap. ; so, ad forum, ap. ; Q. Cic. Petit. cons. 14; Valer. Antias ap. ; ; ; cf.: fuge, quo descendere gestis,; Orell. ad loc.: ad comitia,: de palatio et aedibus suis,.—Absol.: hodie non descendit Antonius,; ; ; —
Transf.: in causam,; ; : in partes,. —
Of land, etc., to sink, fall, slope: regio,.—
Of forests whose wood is brought to the plain, : Caucasus,.—
Of water conveyed in pipes, to fall: subeat descendatque,; cf. of the sea: non magis descenderet aequor,.—
In milit. lang., to march down, sc. from an eminence

into the plain: ex superioribus locis in planitiem,; cf. : qua (sc. de monte),: inde (sc. de arce),; cf. : in aequum locum,; for which, in aequum,: in campum omnibus copiis,: in plana,: ad Alexandriam, et saep.—Absol., ; : ad laevam,—With supine: praedatum in agros Romanos,; .—Hence,

Transf.: in aciem,to go into battle, to engage,; ; : in proelium,; : in certamen,: ad pugnam, ad tales pugnas,; ; ; ; and even, in bellum,; ; cf.: in belli periculum,.—
In medic. lang., of the excrements: to pass off, pass through, : olera,: alvus,.—
Pregn., to sink down, penetrate into any thing (freq. only after the Aug. per.; not in Cic. and Caes.): ferrum in corpus,; cf. : toto descendit in ilia ferro,: (harundo) in caput,; cf.: in jugulos gladiis descendebant (hostes),: ense in jugulos,: in terram (fulmen),: in rimam calamus,: subjacens soli duritia non patitur in altum descendere (radices), lapathi radix ad tria cubita, et saep.: toto corpore pestis,: galeas vetant descendere cristae,to sink down,. —
In an obscene sense, Catull. 112, 2; .—
Trop.
In gen. (esp. freq. in Quint.), to descend, etc.: a vita pastorali ad agriculturam,; cf.: ad aliquem,: usus in nostram aetatem descendit,: (vox) attollitur concitatis affectibus, compositis descendit,; cf. : grammatici omnes in hanc descendent rerum tenuitatem, et saep.: in omnia familiaritatis officia,.—Pass. impers.: eo contemptionis descensum, ut, etc., et saep.: si quid tamen olim Scripseris, in Maeci descendat judicis aures,: si descendere ad ipsum Ordine perpetuo quaeris sunt hujus origo Ilus et Assaracus, etc.,.—
In partic.
(Acc. to no. I. A. 4.) To sink deep into, to penetrate deeply: quod verbum in pectus Jugurthae altius, quam quisquam ratus erat, descendit,; cf.: ut altius injuriae quam merita descendant,; ; : cura in animos Patrum,; cf.: qui (metus deorum) cum descendere ad animos ... non posset,: nemo in sese tentat descendere,to examine himself,.—
To lower one's self, descend to an act or employment, etc.; to yield, agree to any act, esp. to one which is unpleasant or wrong (freq. in Cic. and Caes.; cf. Orell. ad , and Fabri ad ).—Constr. with ad, very rarely with in or absol.: senes ad ludum adolescentium descendant,; cf. : ad calamitatum societates,: sua voluntate sapientem descendere ad rationes civitatis non solere,: ad ejusmodi consilium,: ad innocentium supplicia,fin.: ad vim atque ad arma,: ad gravissimas verborum contumelias,: ad accusandum, ad inimicitias,; ; cf. : ad extrema, Pollio ap. : ad frontis urbanae praemia,: preces in omnes,: videte, quo descendam, judices,; cf. ; : ad intellectum audientis,: ad minutissima opera,; : placet mihi ista defensio; descendo,I acquiesce,.—
(Mostly ante-Aug.) To descend or proceed from any person or thing: ex gradu ascendentium vel descendentium uxorem ducere, et saep.: quod genus liberalitatis ex jure gentium descendit,; cf. : a Platone,; .—Hence, subst.: dē-scendens, entis, m. and f., a descendant;plur. descendentes, posterity, . —
(In Quint.) To depart, deviate, differ from: tantum ab eo defluebat, quantum ille (sc. Seneca) ab antiquis descenderat,; .!*? The passive is very rare, ; .
